slides.title: Software Metrics
bullets: Introduction
“What cannot be measured cannot be Managed"
What does it mean?
without tracking progress and outcomes through data, it's
impossible to make informed decisions or control the direction of a
project, business, or even personal goals.
It emphasizes the importance of metrics for setting benchmarks,
assessing performance, and making necessary adjustments to
improve results.
What are Software Metrics in Software Engineering?
Software metrics in software engineering are the standards for
estimating the quality, progress, and health of software
development activity.
A software metric is a quantifiable or countable assessment of the
qualities of software.

A software metric is a quantifiable or countable assessment of the

slides.title: Software Metrics
bullets: Characteristics of Software Metrics
Software metrics in software engineering should possess the
following characteristics:
➢ Quantitative: Metrics must be quantitative in order to be helpful.
It means that metrics can be stated numerically.
➢ Understandable: Metric computation should be simple
to grasp, and the method for computing them should be well
explained.
➢ Applicability: Metrics should be applied during the early stages
of software development.
➢ Repeatable: When measured regularly and consistently in
nature, the metric values should be the same.
➢ Economical: Metric computation should be cost-effective.
➢ Language agnostic: Metrics should be language-
independent, meaning their computation should not depend on
any programming language.

slides.title: Software Test Measurements
bullets: Note:
Function Points
Function points measure the size of an application system based
on the functional view of the system. The size is determined by
counting the number of inputs, outputs, queries, internal files and
external files in the system and adjusting that total for the functional
complexity of the system.
Function point analysis, originally developed at IBM, has as an
advantage its focus on measuring software produced in terms of
functionality delivered to the end user, rather than in terms of
development deliverables, which have no direct bearing on the end
user.

slides.title: Risks and challenges associated with metrics
bullets: The Streetlight effect
➢ A known observational bias.
➢ People tend to look for something only where it’s easiest to do
so.
➢ If you drop your keys at night, you’ll tend to look for it under
streetlights.
Bad statistics
Making inferences
➢ Provide a theory (from domain knowledge, independent of data)
➢ Show correlation
➢ Demonstrate ability to predict new cases (replicate/validate)
Spurious correlations
Confounding variables

slides.title: Risks and challenges associated with metrics
bullets: Spurious correlations
A spurious correlation occurs when two variables appear to be
statistically related but have no direct causal connection.
A strong correlation might arise from pure chance, a third
confounding factor, or a misinterpretation of complex data. For
software development, this can mean mistaking a side effect for a
primary cause, which can lead to ineffective or even detrimental
changes to development processes.
Example1
Lines of code and bug count: You might observe a strong correlation
between the number of lines of code (LOC) and the number of bugs in a
software module. A novice might conclude that fewer lines of code will
directly cause fewer bugs.
The confounding factor: The actual cause is often the complexity of the
module. A more complex feature requires more code, which in turn
introduces more opportunities for bugs. Simply writing less code does not
reduce bugs; reducing complexity does.

changes to development processes.
Example1
Lines of code and bug count: You might observe a strong correlation
between the number of lines of code (LOC) and the number of bugs in a
software module. A novice might conclude that fewer lines of code will
directly cause fewer bugs.
The confounding factor: The actual cause is often the complexity of the
module. A more complex feature requires more code, which in turn
introduces more opportunities for bugs. Simply writing less code does not
reduce bugs; reducing complexity does.

slides.title: Risks and challenges associated with metrics
bullets: Example 2
Number of features and revenue growth: An optimistic product leader
might observe that as their team releases more features, the company's
revenue also increases. This could lead to a strategy of accelerating
feature development to increase sales.
The confounding factor: The company's overall success—driven by market
demand, effective marketing, and a strong sales team—is the true cause
of the revenue growth. The high feature output and revenue growth are
both results of a well-performing, well-funded business. Simply adding
more features may even make the product more complex and harder for
new users to adopt, potentially hurting growth in the long run.
Example 3
Test coverage and bug reports: A team might notice a high correlation
between increased test coverage and a rise in new bug reports. This could
lead to the incorrect conclusion that adding more tests actually creates
more problems.
The confounding factor: The real cause is a third variable, such as a recent
shift to a more aggressive testing strategy. The new strategy uncovers
many bugs that were already in the code but were previously undetected,
which is the actual purpose of testing.

slides.title: Risks and challenges associated with metrics
bullets: Measurement reliability
Metrics and Incentives
Goodhart’s law: “When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to
be a good measure.”
Incentivizing productivity
What happens when developer bonuses are based on
▪ Lines of code per day?
▪ Amount of documentation written?
▪ Low number of reported bugs in their code?
▪ Low number of open bugs in their code?
▪ High number of fixed bugs?
▪ Accuracy of time estimates?

slides.title: Maintenance - Introduction
bullets: Maintenance: Sustaining process of modifying a software system
or component after delivery, to correct faults, improve performance
or other attributes, or adapt to changed environment
➢ Totality of activities required to provide cost-effective support
to software
➢ Modification of software product after delivery to correct
faults, improve performance or other attributes, or to adapt to
modified environment
➢Largest portion of the total life cycle as products are used for
a long period of time
Why
To ensure software product continues to satisfy customer needs
Commitment to support system, customers have invested in
Who
Maintainer could be an organization or person responsible for
carrying out maintenance activities

Look at future and analyze consequences of solution

slides.title: Techniques or Approaches for Maintenance – Reverse Engineering
bullets: Reverse Engineering:
passive technique to understand a piece of software prior to re-
engineering
▪ Process of recovering specification and design information
about the system from source code
Over time, application may have been corrected, adapted and
enhanced
Application becomes complex, unstable and has unexpected
and serious side effects
Identifies the components of a software product and the
interrelationships between the components
Creates a representation of the software in a different format than
existing code/documentation
Does not modify the product or result in a new product
Typical products of this process are graphs and control flow graphs

slides.title: Techniques or Approaches for Maintenance – Re-Engineering
bullets: Re-Engineering:
process of modifying the software to make it easier to understand,
change and extend
Improving maintainability of system at reasonable cost
Considered from maintenance perspective, when software product
is no longer viable to employ standard maintenance techniques to
support with reasonable efficiency and productivity
May involve Refactoring
Re-Engineered code is expected to result in reduction of CPU
Utilization, Readability, Usability and Performance
Steps
1. Identify current process
2. Document planned reconstruction
3. Reverse engineer
4. Refactor
5. Reconstruct code and data

slides.title: Governance
bullets: Some OSS projects are managed by for-profit firms
➢ Examples: Chromium (Google), Moby (Docker), Ubuntu (Canonical),
TensorFlow (Google), PyTorch (Meta), Java (Oracle)
➢ Contributors may be a mix of employees and community volunteers
➢ Corporations often fund platforms (websites, test servers,
deployments, repository hosting, etc.)
➢ Corporations usually control long-term vision and feature roadmap
Many OSS projects are managed by non-profit foundations or ad-hoc
communities
➢ Examples: Apache Hadoop/Spark/Hbase/Kafka/Tomcat (ASF), Firefox
(Mozilla), Python (PSF), NumPy (community)
➢ Foundations fund project infrastructure via charitable donations
➢ Long-term vision often developed via a collaborative process (e.g.,
Apache) or by benevolent dictators (e.g., Python, Linux)
Corporations still heavily rely on community-owned OSS projects
➢ Many OSS non-profits are funded by Big Tech (e.g., Mozilla by Google)

slides.title: Use of Open Source software within companies
bullets: Is the license compatible with our intended use?
How will we handle versioning and updates?
➢ Does every internal project declare its own versioned dependency or
do we all agree on using one fixed (e.g., latest) version?
➢ Sometimes resolved by assigning internal “owners” of a third-party
dependency, who are responsible for testing updates and declaring
allowable versions.
How to handle customization of the OSS software?
➢ Internal forks are useful but hard to sync with upstream changes.
➢ One option: Assign an internal owner who keeps internal fork up-to-
date with upstream.
➢ Another option: Contribute all customizations back to upstream to
maintain clean dependencies.
Security risks? Supply chain attacks on the rise.

slides.title: Threat Modelling
bullets: What is Privacy Threat Modeling
Privacy threat modeling is an activity to identify potential privacy threats in
an application or system. By performing privacy threat modeling, it is
possible to identify early on in a development process potential risks to
privacy for various stakeholders.
Privacy threat modeling will identify privacy threats so that
countermeasures can be developed before an application or system is in
use.
➢ Applicable to both security and privacy.
➢ A wide variety of possible security and privacy threats.
▪ How can we organize our analysis ?
➢ Basic Idea : Systemic methodology to identify possible threats and
methods to mitigate these threats.
➢ Approach: Use a taxonomy of possible threats.

bullets: Regression testing
➢ Regression testing is testing the system to check that changes
have not ‘broken’ previously working code.
➢ In a manual testing process, regression testing is expensive but,
with automated testing, it is simple and straightforward. All tests
are rerun every time a change is made to the program.
➢ Tests must run ‘successfully’ before the change is committed.

slides.title: More on testing …
bullets: Release testing and system testing
Release testing is a form of system testing.
Important differences:
➢ A separate team that has not been involved in the system
development, should be responsible for release testing.
➢ System testing by the development team should focus on
discovering bugs in the system (defect testing). The
objective of release testing is to check that the system meets
its requirements and is good enough for external use
(validation testing).

slides.title: More on testing …
bullets: Performance testing
Part of release testing may involve testing the emergent properties
of a system, such as performance and reliability.
Tests should reflect the profile of use of the system.
Performance tests usually involve planning a series of tests where
the load is steadily increased until the system performance
becomes unacceptable.
Stress testing is a form of performance testing where the system is
deliberately overloaded to test its failure behaviour.

slides.title: More on testing - Penetration testing
bullets: Penetration testing
Overview
➢ An authorized, simulated cyberattack on a system to evaluate
its security
➢ Goal: identify and exploit vulnerabilities before real attackers do.
➢ Complements other testing (e.g. vulnerability scans) by
mimicking attacker behavior.
➢ Findings include weaknesses in networks, applications,
configurations, or human factors.
➢ Penetration testing (“pentesting”) involves security experts using
the same tools and techniques as attackers to probe a system. It
combines automated scanning with manual exploitation.
➢ The tester reports discovered vulnerabilities and how they can
be exploited, along with recommended fixes.

Overview
➢ An authorized, simulated cyberattack on a system to evaluate

➢ Goal: identify and exploit vulnerabilities before real attackers do.
➢ Complements other testing (e.g. vulnerability scans) by

➢ Penetration testing (“pentesting”) involves security experts using

slides.title: More on testing – Penetration testing
bullets: Types of penetration testing
White-box testing: Tester has full knowledge of target (source
code, architecture)
Black-box testing: Tester knows only public information (like an
external attacker)
Gray-box testing: Tester has partial knowledge (some credentials
or architecture) – a hybrid approach.
Different approaches suit different goals: white-box can be more
thorough by using internal insights, while black-box best simulates a
real external attacker. Gray-box balances both.
Typical industry products (e.g. HW products) go for white box
testing

slides.title: More on testing – Penetration testing process
bullets: ➢ Reconnaissance: Gather information on target (domains, IPs, tech stack) using
public sources (WHOIS, Shodan, etc.) to understand potential attack surfaces
➢ Scanning: Probe the target for open ports, services, and known vulnerabilities
(e.g. using Nmap or vulnerability scanners)
➢ Vulnerability Assessment: Analyze scan results, identify high-risk issues, and
prioritize targets
➢ Exploitation: Attempt to exploit confirmed vulnerabilities (e.g. SQL injection, XSS
(Cross site scripting), misconfigurations) to prove impact and support remediation
planning
➢ Reporting: Document findings, evidence of exploitation, and remediation advice;
often includes screenshots or logs
➢ A typical pentest follows these stages to systematically uncover security flaws.
For example, the Open Web Application Security Project (OWASP) and industry
standards describe similar five-phase methodologies. In exploitation, testers
might demonstrate how an attacker could gain admin access or steal data, which
helps justify fixes.
slides.raw_text:
More on testing – Penetration testing process
➢ Reconnaissance: Gather information on target (domains, IPs, tech stack) using
public sources (WHOIS, Shodan, etc.) to understand potential attack surfaces
➢ Scanning: Probe the target for open ports, services, and known vulnerabilities
(e.g. using Nmap or vulnerability scanners)
➢ Vulnerability Assessment: Analyze scan results, identify high-risk issues, and
prioritize targets
➢ Exploitation: Attempt to exploit confirmed vulnerabilities (e.g. SQL injection, XSS
(Cross site scripting), misconfigurations) to prove impact and support remediation
planning
➢ Reporting: Document findings, evidence of exploitation, and remediation advice;
often includes screenshots or logs
➢ A typical pentest follows these stages to systematically uncover security flaws.
For example, the Open Web Application Security Project (OWASP) and industry
standards describe similar five-phase methodologies. In exploitation, testers
might demonstrate how an attacker could gain admin access or steal data, which
helps justify fixes.

slides.title: More on testing …
bullets: Benefits of penetration testing
Prevents breaches: Finds critical flaws before attackers do.
Compliance and Assurance: Fulfills requirements (e.g. PCI DSS
mandates regular pentests) and boosts stakeholder confidence.
( Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard )
Red Teaming and Risk Assessment: Reveals not just technical
bugs but also process issues (e.g. weak passwords, unpatched
servers) and helps organizations prioritize security improvements.
Pentesting provides a reality check of an organization’s security.
In practice, security audits that include pentesting have helped
companies avoid costly data breaches by uncovering critical flaws
in time.

slides.title: Fuzzing
bullets: Overview
Definition:
Automated testing by feeding a program random, malformed, or
unexpected inputs
Purpose:
Trigger crashes, assertion failures, memory errors, or other bugs that might
be security vulnerabilities.
Key idea:
Let a fuzzer generate many test cases (often continuously) and watch for
faults that manual tests miss.
Fuzzing (or “fuzz testing”) is a dynamic analysis technique. In practice, a
fuzzer iteratively generates inputs and runs the target program, checking if
it crashes or behaves incorrectly
Unlike traditional test suites with fixed cases, fuzzers explore thousands to
millions of inputs, including edge cases and random data. This exposes
hidden bugs, especially in low-level code (e.g. C/C++ memory errors) or
poorly-validated parsers.

Fuzzing
Overview
Definition:
Automated testing by feeding a program random, malformed, or
unexpected inputs
Purpose:
Trigger crashes, assertion failures, memory errors, or other bugs that might
be security vulnerabilities.
Key idea:
Let a fuzzer generate many test cases (often continuously) and watch for
faults that manual tests miss.
Fuzzing (or “fuzz testing”) is a dynamic analysis technique. In practice, a
fuzzer iteratively generates inputs and runs the target program, checking if
it crashes or behaves incorrectly
Unlike traditional test suites with fixed cases, fuzzers explore thousands to
millions of inputs, including edge cases and random data. This exposes
hidden bugs, especially in low-level code (e.g. C/C++ memory errors) or
poorly-validated parsers.

slides.title: Types of fuzzers
bullets: Mutation-based fuzzers: Start from valid sample inputs and modify them
(flip bits, alter lengths, insert special values)
Generation-based fuzzers: Use a model of the input format (specification
or grammar) to generate new inputs from scratch.
White-box fuzzers: Have full knowledge of the target (source
code/structure); can use e.g. symbolic execution or instrumentation.
Gray-box fuzzers: Use feedback (e.g. code coverage) but treat the target
as a black-box binary with limited instrumentation.
Black-box fuzzers: No knowledge of internals; treat the program purely as
an external interface, relying on random inputs only.
Many fuzzers fall on a spectrum of intelligence. For example, a “dumb”
fuzzer might choose purely random bytes, while a “smart” fuzzer tries to
produce syntactically valid or interesting inputs. In fact, fuzzers can be
categorized by how much they know: white-box fuzzers know internal
details, black-box know nothing, and gray-box have some instrumentation.

slides.title: Fuzzing process
bullets: Input Generation: The fuzzer produces test cases (either by mutating seed inputs
or generating new data)
Program Execution: Each test input is fed to the target program, which is run under
a monitor (often with sanitizers like AddressSanitizer) to detect errors.
Monitoring/Analysis: The fuzzer watches for crashes, hangs, leaks, or assertion
failures. It logs inputs that cause such failures.
Feedback-Driven Loop: Coverage-guided fuzzers analyze which new code paths
were exercised. Inputs that increase coverage are “favored” and used to generate
further mutations
Modern fuzzers operate in three phases: they generate inputs, run the target, and
then use the results to drive further testing. For instance, AFL and libFuzzer track
execution to find new branches.
Fuzz testing steps (generate or mutate inputs, run the target, monitor for crashes,
and analyze failures) are repeated thousands of times to uncover crashes or
vulnerabilities.

slides.title: Fuzzing - value
bullets: Uncovers deep bugs: Fuzzing has found countless memory safety and
crash bugs in critical software (e.g. browsers, SSL libraries) that were
invisible to code review
Broad applicability: It can test anything with a programmable interface:
libraries, file parsers, network servers, even entire kernel modules.
Continuous security: Services like Google’s OSS-Fuzz continuously fuzz
open-source projects and report new CVEs, fixing bugs before users find
them.
Complements other testing: Unlike pentesting (which targets high-level
behavior), fuzzing excels at low-level code paths. Together they strengthen
security validation.
Fuzzing is especially valuable for security validation because it simulates
random/malicious inputs.

slides.title: Fuzzing tools – Open Source
bullets: AFL / AFL++ (C/C++): A coverage-guided mutation fuzzer; widely used.
libFuzzer (C/C++): A library-based fuzzer integrated into LLVM/Clang; generates
inputs in-process using sanitizers.
Honggfuzz (C): A general-purpose feedback-driven fuzzer supporting sanitizers and
code-coverage.
Syzkaller (C, Linux Kernel): Kernel fuzzer by Google, uses system call models to
fuzz the Linux kernel.
Radamsa: A gray-box dumb mutational fuzzer (common for file-format fuzzing).
Hypothesis (Python): A property-based testing library – part of the lab later on.
Python fuzzers: e.g. BooFuzz (network protocol fuzzer), python-afl (bindings for
AFL), PyFuzzer packages.
There are many open-source fuzzers. For C/C++ code, AFL and libFuzzer are
standards. Google’s OSS-Fuzz runs large-scale fuzzing on thousands of projects
(finding ~10,000 bugs since launch). Python has its own ecosystem.

slides.title: Fuzzing – case studies
bullets: Mozilla Firefox (2022–2023): Mozilla’s fuzzers detected 20
vulnerabilities (5 critical, 15 high) in Firefox 102/103, such as memory
safety bugs, before these versions shipped
OpenSSL (2022): Google’s OSS-Fuzz found two critical CVEs (CVE-2022-
3602, CVE-2022-3786) – stack buffer overflows in the Punycode parser.
These were fixed before public exploitation
Linux Kernel: The Syzkaller project has unearthed thousands of kernel
bugs since 2015, many being privilege escalations (e.g. CVE-2023-0386).
Other: Tools like AFL have been used to fuzz browsers (Chrome/Firefox),
PDF readers, media libraries, often yielding dozens of CVEs each year.
These examples (all within 5 years) highlight fuzzing’s impact. They show
that even mature, critical software still benefits from automated fuzzing.
Many companies now integrate fuzzing into their CI pipelines for this
reason.

slides.title: Stubs
bullets: What's a Stub?
➢ A controllable replacement for a software unit. Used to simulate
difficult-to-control elements or components not yet developed
Why you need them:
➢ Component B doesn't exist yet (you're still building it)
➢ Component B is hard to control (it's a 3rd-party service,
database, network)
➢ Component B is slow (real database calls take time)
➢ Component B has side effects (sending emails, charging cards)
Example: Testing registration logic without touching real database:
➢ Create a StubDatabase that returns fake data
➢ Registration logic can be tested in isolation
➢ No risk of data corruption
Key point: Minimize code changes when you remove the stub.

slides.title: PCMM
bullets: What’s PCMM?
The People Capability Maturity Model (P-CMM) is a framework
developed by Carnegie Mellon University to help organizations
improve their human resource practices and continuously develop
their workforce's knowledge, skills, and motivation.
